2. When a user program needs an OS service (file read, create process) it makes a system call → a trap instruction sets the mode
 bit to 0 and jumps to the kernel routine.

program cannot loop forever); safe access to I/O. Example: a program calling read() executes in user mode until the system-call
trap, runs inside the kernel in kernel mode while the disk driver works, and then returns to user mode. Systems such as Intel x86
extend this idea to 4 rings (ring 0 = kernel … ring 3 = user), and virtualisation adds an extra hypervisor mode.

 Q1 (c) [5 marks]

 What is deadlock prevention? Discuss any two strategies used for preventing deadlocks in an operating system.


 Deadlock prevention is a set of methods that ensure at least one of the four necessary conditions cannot hold, so a
 deadlock can never occur. It works by constraining how requests for resources are made (it is a static, conservative approach,
 unlike avoidance which examines the resource-allocation state dynamically, e.g. Banker's algorithm).


Strategy 1 – Eliminate Hold and Wait
Guarantee that when a process requests a resource it does not hold any other resource. Two protocols: (a) a process must
request and be allocated all its resources before it begins execution; (b) a process may request resources only when it has none
– it must release everything before asking for more.
Disadvantages: low resource utilisation (resources held but unused for a long time), possible starvation (a process needing many
popular resources may wait forever), and processes may not know their needs in advance.

Strategy 2 – Eliminate Circular Wait (resource ordering)
Impose a total ordering on all resource types (e.g. tape = 1, disk = 5, printer = 12) and require each process to request resources
only in increasing order of this number. A cycle then cannot form because a process holding Rj can never wait for an Ri with i < j.
Disadvantage: the ordering may not match the natural usage order, wasting resources; programmers must follow the order
strictly. This is the most practical prevention method (used for lock ordering in kernels).

Other strategies
 Eliminate No-Pre-emption: if a process holding resources requests one that is not available, all its held resources are pre-
 empted (released) and it restarts only when it can get everything; or take resources from a waiting process. Works for CPU
 registers/memory but not printers or tapes.

 Eliminate Mutual Exclusion: make resources shareable (read-only files); not possible for intrinsically non-sharable ones
 (printer), so it is rarely applicable (spooling helps).

 Paging is a non-contiguous memory-management scheme in which the physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks
 called frames and the logical (process) address space into blocks of the same size called pages. Pages of a process can be
 loaded into any free frames, and a page table maps each page to its frame.

Purpose of paging
 Allows the physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous – a process can be allocated memory wherever it is
 available.
 Eliminates external fragmentation (only a little internal fragmentation in the last page).

 Avoids the problem of fitting varying-sized chunks into backing store; makes virtual memory possible; supports sharing
 (shared pages) and protection (valid/invalid and read/write bits in the page table).

Address translation
Every logical address generated by the CPU is divided into: page number (p) – index into the page table; page offset (d) –
displacement within the page. If logical address space = 2m and page size = 2n, then the high-order m − n bits are p and the low-
order n bits are d.

 1. CPU generates logical address (p, d).

 2. p is used as an index into the page table (base address held in the PTBR) to get the frame number f.

 3. Physical address = f × (page size) + d, i.e. f is concatenated with d.

 4. The valid/invalid bit is checked; invalid → trap (page fault / protection error).

Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB)
With the page table in main memory every data access needs two memory accesses (one for the page-table entry, one for the
data) – this halves speed. The TLB is a small, very fast associative (content-addressable) hardware cache (typically 64–1024
entries) that stores recently used page → frame mappings. Each entry has key (page #) and value (frame #); all entries are
searched in parallel.

 TLB hit: page number found in TLB → frame number available immediately → only one memory access (plus a TLB lookup of a
 few ns).
 TLB miss: the page table in memory is consulted (extra access), and the entry is loaded into the TLB (replacement policy
 LRU/random) for future use.
 On a context switch the TLB is flushed, or entries carry an ASID (address-space identifier) so that several processes can share
 it.
